source.title: Towards Understanding the Nature of Attention with Low-Rank Sparse Decomposition
source.authors: Zheng-Fu He; Junxuan Wang; Rui Lin; Xu-Yang Ge; Wentao Shu; Qiong Tang; Junping Zhang; Xi-Peng Qiu

page_placements.theme: Attention heads: monosemantic vs polysemantic roles

record.tranche_reason: The study discusses neuron superposition by analogy but evaluates sparse attention units and SAE features, not individual neuron explanations or neuron-pole job counts.
record.gate_note: The study reports automated interpretability results for Lorsa heads and attention-output SAE features. Those results are recorded as adjacent evidence, not as tests of the neuron-specific claim versions. It also mentions neuron findings from other work; those cited findings are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study builds and evaluates Lorsa, a sparse replacement for attention, and scores Lorsa heads and attention-output SAE features with automated interpretability in Pythia-160M. It reports no rates or scores for individual MLP neurons, no neuron-pole audit, and no neuron-based attribution graphs. Its neuron statements in Section 2 cite prior work (Gurnee, Bricken, Arora) rather than its own results. So none of its results bears on V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that Lorsa recovers known attention mechanisms and uncovers new interpretable heads, such as arithmetic-specific heads. Its automated interpretability is on par with SAE features. Shared QK circuits and remaining superposition are the key open challenges.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a sparse replacement for attention and evaluates Lorsa heads and SAE features; it does not use the neuron-pole auditing or neuron-explanation scoring methods in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Automated interpretability scores descend in deeper layers for both Lorsa and SAE features.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia-160M, GPT-4o simulation scores for Lorsa heads matched attention-output SAE features (6 wins, 3 losses, 15 ties over 24 comparisons). Scores for both declined in deeper layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse attention units are about as interpretable as attention-output SAE features by automated simulation scoring, and both score lower in deeper layers.

fits_no_version.finding: About half of Lorsa heads draw mainly on one original MHSA head; the rest are spread across two or more heads (Appendix F.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A substantial share of attention units are spread across multiple MHSA heads (attention superposition).

record.problems: The automated interpretability evaluation samples 100 heads/features per distribution; absolute score values are presented in a figure rather than stated in the text. The authors also note that autointerpretability may have limited capacity for long-range dependencies.
record.rows_left_out: No other qualifying rows. The paper's neuron examples and neuron-head interpretability statements in Section 2 cite prior work rather than reporting this study's own neuron results.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job shares.
No neuron job shares across models or scale.
No study of InceptionV1 or of canonical polysemantic neurons; it only cites prior polysemantic neuron reports.
No measurement of how the share of interpretable neurons changes with architecture or tools.
Its attribution graph uses Lorsa and Transcoder replacements in a 2-layer model, not a large model's own neurons.
No test of whether neuron explanations predict firing.
Simulation scoring is applied to Lorsa heads and SAE features, not neurons; it reports no fraction of well-scored neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The record's not_tested assessments are accurate. The Appendix F.2 finding on how Lorsa heads spread across MHSA heads concerns attention, not neurons, so it is added only under fits_no_version. Remaining unrecorded appendix results (ablations, scaling law, dark matter) are Lorsa method results with no bearing on V1–V7.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or report shares of poles with one, two, or unknown jobs.
Does not measure neuron-pole job shares across models, architectures, or scale.
Does not study the InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or recursive generalization.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares in vision models or test architecture, regularization, or tool effects on those shares.
Its attribution-graph example uses Lorsa and Transcoder in a two-layer Transformer, not a large model's own neurons; it does not test the stated neuron-based reconstruction claim.
Does not test whether explanations of individual neurons fit activating examples but fail to predict their firing.
Automated interpretability is applied to Lorsa heads and SAE features, not individual neuron explanations; the text does not report the fraction of neuron explanations receiving good scores.
